name: Yusuf Okafor

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to employers, AI firms, unions or government. Your answers stay confidential. What does a normal workday look like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I am the senior person on a line crew that does new connections and emergency repairs for the electricity company. The two-year diploma gave me the theory; what I teach younger workers is to pause when the pole, plan and meter disagree. I use AI now and then to turn rough notes into a clear handover, but I read the result aloud before the next shift gets it. My partner Anika and I have two school-age children, a mortgage and about four months of expenses saved, so we can handle a short gap but not a lost career.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the crew a better handover sheet is welcome if it carries the actual meter values. Our work is still putting a safe connection on the pole, not making the form look tidy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The mild change would leave my typical wage and shifts mostly alone. Four months saved means the mortgage would survive a short interruption, but I do not want an error passed between shifts under my name.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep the present rota and compare the AI handover with my notebook before sending it. In the first year I would ask the incoming crew to mark one unclear handover so I could improve the template.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm about the job, though I still feel responsible for a clean handoff. The quickest report is not always the clearest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the incoming crew mark?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They should circle a missing meter value or an unclear switch position. I would rather get a blunt note at breakfast than a call from the wrong pole at noon.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you use the tool more often?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only if those handovers come back clearer. I try new software after it proves useful to the next person, not because an office notice calls it clever.

say: **AI handovers** help the next line crew when every meter value and switch position remains visible.
**Safe connections** matter more than polished forms.
think: My **typical pay** and shifts should continue in this mild picture.
A wrong **handover** could still carry my name into the next crew’s work.
do: **Keep** the current connection and repair rota.
**Check** each AI handover against notebook values and revise one unclear template.
feel: **Calm** about income, attentive to handover quality.
S0.quote: I would rather get a blunt note at breakfast than a call from the wrong pole at noon.
fieldNote: He is **steady** about technology, adopting it when a later crew finds it useful.
His **four-month cushion** protects a short gap, while his main concern is work quality.

steps.text: Keep present line connection and repair rota
Check AI handovers against notebook and improve unclear template

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say dispatch and ordering may lose tasks first, but the field crew will still need to climb and test. I would ask for the union and dispatchers to sit with us before the company changes repair targets.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I can see the benefit of faster fault calls, yet fewer dispatchers might mean a missing detail lands on our truck. If that cuts callouts or stretches our shift without pay, the mortgage budget would tighten even with four months saved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would trial the proposed route plan on five faults and write down where access or switching takes longer. In the first year I would bring that log with a dispatcher to the union safety meeting, then ask for a target that counts the full job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, not hostile. I would like the tool to work, but I want the dispatcher who knows the streets in the room.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which missing detail would matter?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A caller may know that the rear lane floods, while the map only shows a road. A dispatcher who asks one more question can save the crew a wasted drive.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the trial shows faster work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would sign the log and say so. Then I would still ask whether the company plans to cut a dispatcher or just serve customers sooner.

say: **Field repair** remains physical while dispatch and ordering change first.
**Joint review** with dispatchers and union representatives should precede new targets.
think: A lost **street detail** could make the crew waste time.
We could face **tighter pay** if the company trims callouts or extends shifts.
do: **Trial** five AI route plans against real access and switching time.
**Bring** the log with a dispatcher to the union safety meeting.
feel: **Uneasy**, yet willing to credit a tool that works.
S1.quote: A dispatcher who asks one more question can save the crew a wasted drive.
fieldNote: He seeks a **joint review** with dispatchers, not only a crew complaint.
His **five-fault trial** would log faster as well as slower results before he presses for target changes.

steps.text: Trial five AI routes against crew access and switching times
Bring route log with dispatcher to union safety meeting

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the apprentices that full thinking AI by 2028 changes the plans and call desk before fully capable field robots arrive about 2031. The three years between are still real work, and we should use them to learn what machines get wrong.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A robot may eventually do the climb I am paid for, and four months of savings will not carry the family through a long search. Some other utilities are nearby, but I would expect many of them to be asking the same question about crew numbers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask the company to let senior lineworkers observe a robot test and request a written count of planned field jobs. If a paid protection-testing course leads to a real local opening, I would enrol; after 2028 I would apply for that work and put extra callout pay toward the mortgage while shifts continue.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious and wide awake. I have a runway of about three years for the physical work, but it is shorter than a mortgage term.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you look for at a robot test?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would watch how it handles an old pole with fittings that do not match the drawing. A tidy robot demonstration on a new power line would tell me very little.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How much extra would go to the mortgage?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only callout pay above our usual household budget, if I earn it. I would not use the four-month emergency fund to make an extra payment.

say: **2028 thinking AI** reaches planning before capable field robots around 2031.
**Old poles** belong in robot tests, not just new equipment.
think: Our **four-month buffer** would not fund a long job search.
Nearby **utility jobs** may shrink at the same time as ours.
do: **Observe** a field robot test and seek a written job count.
**Enrol** in paid protection testing only for a real local vacancy.
**Apply** after 2028 and pay extra on the mortgage from earned surplus callouts.
feel: **Anxious**, with a short field-work runway to prepare.
S2.quote: A tidy robot demonstration on a new power line would tell me very little.
fieldNote: He tests the **robot scenario** against old hardware and messy field conditions.
His **plans** for training, a job move and extra debt payment depend on funding, vacancy and actual earnings.

steps.text: Observe field robot test on old poles
Enrol in paid protection testing if a real local vacancy exists
Apply for local protection testing after 2028 if trained
Pay extra on mortgage from earned surplus callouts

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With five years, I would ask the utility to run a proper field trial before thinking AI arrives in 2031. Robots able to repair lines follow around 2034, so we could test them through several bad-weather seasons.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I am willing to learn a tested system, but I will not promise to leave the crew for an unknown wage. Our children will be older then and the mortgage may still be substantial, even if we keep our four-month reserve.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask our union branch and the training manager to publish the field-trial results and the pay scale for protection testing. If a paid course and a local vacancy at a bill-covering wage are offered, I would train before 2031 and apply during the first year after 2031; otherwise I would keep the crew role.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Careful, but encouraged by the time. A working field robot trial and a written protection-testing wage would turn a frightening guess into a decision.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would count as a working trial?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The robot should handle storm damage on an older line and stop when the isolation reading is uncertain. The crew should log the failure and the repair time alongside any successful runs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would your partner back the testing role?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anika would want to compare the wage and hours with school pickup and our mortgage payment. I think she would back it if the figures worked, but I cannot decide for her.

say: **Field trials** should span difficult weather before robots arrive around 2034.
**Published results** and wages would make a job decision possible.
think: I will learn a **tested system** but not leave the crew for unknown pay.
The **mortgage and children** will still shape our choice in five years.
do: **Request** published field results and protection-testing pay scale through the union.
**Complete** paid training before 2031 only for a local bill-covering vacancy.
**Apply** for testing after 2031 if qualified; otherwise keep crew shifts.
feel: **Careful**, with more confidence if evidence and wages are written down.
S3.quote: A working field robot trial and a written protection-testing wage would turn a frightening guess into a decision.
fieldNote: He requires **field evidence** and pay terms before committing to a new role.
His **partner’s view** matters, but he does not claim to know her answer for certain.

steps.text: Ask union branch for published robot trial results and testing pay scale
Complete paid protection-testing course if local bill-covering vacancy exists
Apply for protection-testing role after 2031 if qualified

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A decade gives us time to teach apprentices how to check both the wire and the machine report. Thinking AI in 2036 and field robots around 2039 leave room for crews to write proper stop rules.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At fifty-three I may still want the physical work, although callouts can wear a person down. I cannot assume retirement or a paid-off mortgage, but a well-paid role checking field machines could give me a gentler last stretch.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep leading the crew and review our mortgage and savings with Anika each year. In the first year after 2036 I would apply for a local machine-inspection role if it offers paid training and enough wage for our bills; I would help the union crew committee draft a stop rule before the robots come.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fairly steady. The longer horizon lets me plan a change without gambling the household on it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What should the stop rule say?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Any crew member who sees a bad isolation reading can halt a robot and record the reason. A manager should have to inspect the robot fault before restarting the machine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the inspection role is not offered?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would stay on repairs while there is work and keep reviewing the mortgage. I would not spend our four-month reserve on a course without a job to use it in.

say: **Apprentices** should check wires and machine reports together.
**Crew stop rules** need to be ready before field robots arrive around 2039.
think: A **machine-inspection role** could reduce hard callouts if it pays enough.
I cannot assume **retirement** or a paid-off mortgage at fifty-three.
do: **Review** mortgage and savings with Anika each year while leading repairs.
**Apply** for local inspection after 2036 only with paid training and bill-covering pay.
**Draft** a robot stop rule through the union crew committee.
feel: **Steady**, with time to test a possible career change.
S4.quote: A manager should have to inspect the robot fault before restarting the machine.
fieldNote: He treats **inspection** as paid work, with training and wage conditions.
His **long runway** supports annual debt review and collective safety rulemaking, not early retirement.

steps.text: Keep leading repairs and review mortgage with Anika annually
Apply for local machine inspection after 2036 only with paid training and bill-covering pay
Draft robot stop rule through union crew committee

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most, because thinking work would change before the field crews can see which jobs remain when robots arrive around 2031. A paid course linked to a real local testing post and clear trial results would help.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn’t ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You did not ask who has to explain a failed robot repair to the next shift. I would want the robot repair failure in the handover with the meter reading, not hidden in a summary.

portrait: **Yusuf Okafor**, 43, leads a power line crew and has a two-year technical diploma.
He and partner Anika have **two school-age children**, a mortgage, typical lineworker pay and about four months of expenses saved.
He uses **AI occasionally** for handovers, adopting tools once field results prove they help the next crew.
During **Steady Disruption**, he tests routes with dispatchers and brings the findings to a union safety meeting.
The **2028 scenario** worries him most; longer runways allow conditional training and a possible local inspection move.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** leaves only about three years before capable field robots could shrink line crew work.
whatWouldHelp: A **paid course** tied to a real local protection-testing post would make a move credible.
Published **field trials** and clear stop rules would let crews judge robot safety.
headlineQuote: I would want the robot repair failure in the handover with the meter reading, not hidden in a summary.
